title: Friendship made it fun (2.8–2.9)
hookLine: he wouldn't have stolen the pears alone; the gang made it sweet
tomorrow: what was singing in his ears when he got to Carthage?

cards: A car full of friends at midnight, the windows down, and somebody says, let's go. Nobody really decides. The laughter decides.

You met Augustine's version of that night back on day seven hundred thirty-four: a few boys, a pear tree, and his question, why did I do it? Book two keeps circling a narrower question. Would he have done it alone?

teach.b: He goes over it the way you might reread an old message. What did I love in that theft? Not the pears; he had better ones at home.

Alone, he says, he wouldn't have done it, and alone it would have been no fun. What he loved was the company. Then he tries to describe the laughter itself, a tickle in the heart at fooling owners who had no idea.
Hardly anyone laughs alone, he notices; the group makes the laugh. And then the line that stings.
The moment someone said let's go, let's do it, he was ashamed not to be shameless. He has a name for that kind of friendship.
In Pusey's translation: "O friendship too unfriendly!" A friendship that wasn't one. Here's what lifts it above a confession of mischief.
Augustine never decides friends are the problem.
The pull of a group works both ways. The same longing to belong that carried a boy to a pear tree can carry someone toward goodness, if the people beside him are going there.
Proverbs says it plainly: walk with the wise and you'll grow wise; befriend fools and you'll become like them. So the question isn't whether to have friends.
It's where they're walking, and whether you'd walk there alone.

how: Catholics speak of spiritual friendship, and parishes offer small groups, prayer partners and sponsors for the sacraments, so that people walk alongside others who help them grow.

games.q: what does “friendship made it fun” mean?
o: the gang, not the pears, made the theft sweet
a fun time shared with friends after school
friends make every good thing more enjoyable

games.q: the pear tree — tap the pairs.
p: walk with the wise, grow wise

s: Augustine stole the pears because he was hungry
he says the pears were nothing to him. what he loved was the company.
Augustine says he wouldn't have done it alone
alone, he says, it would have been no fun.
Augustine decides friendship itself is the problem
he names a friendship too unfriendly. the pull of company works both ways.

games.q: your study group always ends up mocking one classmate. on your own you'd never do it. what fits Augustine's point?
o: the group's pull works both ways: steer it, or step out.
groups are the problem; study alone from now on.
it's harmless if everyone does it together.
games.why: Augustine doesn't give up on friends. he asks where they're walking, and whether he'd walk there alone.

practice: If there's a piece of fruit nearby, pick it up: feel its weight, smell the skin. Augustine says the pears themselves were nothing to him; the company was the flavor.

Holding the fruit, bring to mind one friend whose company pulls you toward the person you hope to be, and stay with that face until the sit ends. Anyone who prays can give thanks for that friend by name.

wordCard.voice: Friendship made it fun. Augustine's admission that he'd never have stolen the pears alone: the gang made it sweet.

orig.note: Latin, Confessions 2.9: let's go, let's do it.

carryVoice: Keep this one: not alone, because the company you keep carries a person either way. Go gently.
